scenes.label: Long Walk
scenes.line: Evers and his siblings walked 12 miles a day to attend segregated schools. In 1943, Medgar Evers enlisted in the United States Army at age seventeen. Evers served in the 657th Port Company, a segregated unit of the Army.
scenes.image_prompt: Children walking along a dusty road., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Normandy Landings
scenes.line: He participated in the Normandy landings in June 1944 as part of this unit. Evers' unit was part of the Red Ball Express delivering supplies to Allied troops. During his Army time, Evers was angered by the segregation and mistreatment of Black troops.
scenes.image_prompt: A military landing craft approaching a beach., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Changing Perspectives
scenes.line: Serving as a military policeman and dating a white French woman changed his perspective. Evers was honorably discharged from the Army in 1946 with the rank of technician fifth grade. After returning home, Evers enrolled at Alcorn Agricultural and Mechanical College in 1948.
scenes.image_prompt: A military police officer on duty in a European city., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Campus Life
scenes.line: He majored in business administration and participated on debate and football teams. On December 24, 1951, Evers married his classmate Myrlie Beasley. Evers and his wife moved to Mound Bayou, Mississippi, a town developed by African Americans.
scenes.image_prompt: Students engaged in a debate., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Salesman Role
scenes.line: Evers became a salesman for T. R. M. Howard's Magnolia Mutual Life Insurance Company. He became active in the civil rights movement, serving as president of the Regional Council of Negro Leadership. The RCNL organized actions to end segregation, including boycotting certain gasoline stations.
scenes.image_prompt: A man in a suit making a sales pitch., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Large Conferences
scenes.line: Evers attended RCNL conferences that drew crowds of 10,000 or more people. Following the 1954 Supreme Court ruling, Evers applied to the University of Mississippi Law School. His application was rejected due to his race as the school had long been segregated.
scenes.image_prompt: A large outdoor gathering of people., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: NAACP Field Secretary
scenes.line: On November 24, 1954, Evers was named the NAACP's first field secretary for Mississippi. In this position, he helped organize boycotts and establish new local NAACP chapters. Evers encouraged Dr. Gilbert Mason Sr. in organizing the Biloxi wade-ins against beach segregation.
scenes.image_prompt: A building with an NAACP sign., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Integrating Facilities
scenes.line: He also worked to integrate Jackson's privately owned buses and public parks. Evers led voter registration drives and used boycotts to integrate Leake County schools. Local whites founded the White Citizens' Council to resist the integration of schools and facilities.
scenes.image_prompt: A city bus at a stop., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Increased Hostility
scenes.line: In the weeks before his death, Evers encountered new levels of hostility. On May 28, 1963, a Molotov cocktail was thrown into the carport of his home. Ten days later, Evers was nearly run over by a car after leaving the NAACP office.
scenes.image_prompt: An angry crowd gathered., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Constant Threat
scenes.line: Evers lived with the constant threat of death from those opposing civil rights. Before his death, Evers and his wife had trained their children for attacks. On June 12, 1963, Evers pulled into his driveway after returning from a meeting.
scenes.image_prompt: A person looking over their shoulder., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Carrying T-shirts
scenes.line: Emerging from his car, Evers was carrying T-shirts that read 'Jim Crow Must Go'. He was struck in the back with a bullet fired from a rifle. Evers rose and staggered 30 feet before collapsing outside his front door.
scenes.image_prompt: A person holding folded t-shirts., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Wife's Discovery
scenes.line: His wife, Myrlie, was the first to find him after the shooting. Evers was taken to a hospital in Jackson following the shooting. Medgar Wiley Evers died at 1:20 am the following day.
scenes.image_prompt: A woman discovering someone on the ground., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: National Mourning
scenes.line: Evers was mourned nationally and buried on June 19 in Arlington National Cemetery. He received full military honors at his burial before a crowd of over 3,000 people. An estimated 5,000 people marched from the Masonic Temple to the Collins Funeral Home.
scenes.image_prompt: A solemn procession of mourners., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Arrest of Killer
scenes.line: Byron De La Beckwith was arrested for Evers' murder on June 21, 1963. All-white juries in 1964 deadlocked on De La Beckwith's guilt and failed to reach a verdict. In 1994, De La Beckwith was prosecuted again based on new evidence.
scenes.image_prompt: Police officers leading a suspect away., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Body Exhumed
scenes.line: During the trial, the body of Evers was exhumed for an autopsy. On February 5, 1994, De La Beckwith was convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison. In 1969, Medgar Evers College was established in Brooklyn, New York.
scenes.image_prompt: A shovel near a grave site., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Widow's Activism
scenes.line: Evers' widow Myrlie became a noted activist and served as national chairperson of the NAACP. In 1969, Medgar's brother Charles was elected mayor of Fayette, Mississippi, the first African American mayor in the state. On June 28, 1992, the city of Jackson, Mississippi erected a statue in honor of Evers.
scenes.image_prompt: A woman speaking at a podium., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.label: Airport Renamed
scenes.line: In December 2004, the city's airport was renamed Jackson–Medgar Wiley Evers International Airport. In 2017, the Medgar and Myrlie Evers House was named as a National Historic Landmark. Two years later, the site was designated a National Monument.

scenes.image_prompt: A large cargo ship at sea., cinematic, epic, historically accurate, vibrant colors, dramatic lighting, 4K

scenes.line: In 2024, Evers was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Joe Biden.

scenes.line: Mohammad Abdus Salam was a Pakistani theoretical physicist and Nobel laureate who achieved international recognition. He shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physics with Steven Weinberg and Sheldon Glashow for scientific contributions.

scenes.label: Electroweak Theory

scenes.label: Physics Founder
